hooks.text: The first photo from Venus showed daylight bright enough to read by.
An armored titanium sphere plunged into ninety atmospheres of crushing pressure.
Sixty-six kilograms of machinery took the first image on another world.

title: The First Photograph Ever Taken on the Surface of Venus
description: Discover how the Soviet Venera 9 mission captured the first picture from the surface of Venus in 1975.

beats.text: The first photo from Venus showed daylight bright enough to read by.
beats.visual: Venera 9 original panoramic surface photograph of Venus, 1975

beats.text: On October 22, 1975, a Soviet lander touched down in the upland volcanic region of Beta Regio.
beats.visual: Beta Regio topographic radar scan of Venus by Magellan, 1991

beats.text: Scientists anticipated a pitch-black wasteland crushed under ninety atmospheres of pressure.
beats.visual: Venus full disk in ultraviolet light by Mariner 10, 1974

beats.text: Instead, the 660-kilogram armored sphere came to rest on a twenty-degree volcanic slope.
beats.visual: Venera 9 lander model in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics, 1975
queries: Venera lander Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics

beats.text: Sunlight filtered through dense clouds, illuminating flat, sharp-edged rocks never worn smooth by wind.
beats.visual: Venera 9 surface panorama showing flat volcanic slabs, 1975

beats.text: Although a protective lens cover failed to separate, the lander operated for fifty-three minutes.
beats.visual: Venera 9 spacecraft bus and orbiter diagram, 1975

beats.text: Transmissions ended only when the relay orbiter drifted out of radio range below the horizon.
beats.visual: Soviet postage stamp commemorating Venera 9 mission, 1975

beats.text: That shocking view proved that daylight bright enough to read by existed on Venus.
beats.visual: Venera 9 surface panorama detail of volcanic rocks, 1975
